questions.question:
Under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, security responsibilities are divided between AWS and the customer. A web application is being deployed on Amazon EC2 to serve customer data.

Which of the following is the responsibility of AWS?

choices.text: Installing and patching the operating system on EC2 instances
choices.explanation: Customers are responsible for patching the guest operating system and applications running on EC2 instances; AWS manages the hypervisor level.

choices.text: Configuring security groups and network access control lists (NACLs)
choices.explanation: Configuring security groups and NACLs is the customer's responsibility for their deployed resources.

choices.text: Encrypting data stored in application databases
choices.explanation: While AWS provides encryption tools, customers are responsible for choosing and implementing encryption for their application data.

choices.text: Maintaining the physical security of data center facilities and hardware infrastructure
choices.explanation: AWS is responsible for the physical infrastructure, including data center security, power systems, and hardware maintenance.

skills: 2.1.1: Recognizing the components of the AWS shared responsibility model.
questions.tip: Consider what AWS controls at the infrastructure level versus what customers control on their deployed resources.
questions.explanation:
AWS is responsible for the security OF the cloud—physical infrastructure, power, cooling, and host security. Customers are responsible for security IN the cloud, including OS patching, firewall rules, and application-level encryption.

**Why it works:** AWS manages all physical data center components and hardware; this is fundamental to their infrastructure responsibility.

**Why the others fail:**
- Configuring security groups/NACLs: These are customer-managed network controls on deployed resources.
- Installing/patching the OS: Customers manage the guest OS; AWS manages only the hypervisor level.
- Encrypting application data: Customers choose and implement encryption strategies for their data.

**Implementation:** Review AWS Shared Responsibility Model documentation at https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/shared-responsibility-model/

questions.question:
Compliance archives accessed approximately once per quarter for audits must be retained for 10 years under a limited storage budget.

Which storage option provides the lowest cost for this use case?

choices.text: EBS Snapshots
choices.explanation: EBS Snapshots are for block storage snapshots, not suitable for long-term archived data retention.

choices.text: S3 Standard
choices.explanation: Standard is significantly more expensive than Archive solutions for long-term retention.

choices.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
choices.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering is more expensive than Deep Archive for data with infrequent predictable access.

choices.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
choices.explanation: Deep Archive offers the lowest storage cost ($1.26/TB/month) and supports compliance retention with quarterly retrieval patterns.

skills: 4.1.5: Understanding different pricing options for various storage options and tiers.
questions.tip: For long-term, infrequently accessed compliance data, consider the cheapest storage class even with retrieval delays.
questions.explanation:
S3 Glacier Deep Archive minimizes storage costs for compliance archives with quarterly access.

**Why it works:** Deep Archive charges approximately $1.26/TB/month with a 12-hour retrieval window—acceptable for quarterly compliance audits.

**Why the others fail:**
- S3 Standard: Costs 10x more than Deep Archive for inactive compliance data
- Intelligent-Tiering: More expensive than Deep Archive for predictable infrequent access
- EBS Snapshots: Designed for database backups, not long-term data retention

**Implementation:** Move compliance archives to Deep Archive via lifecycle rules after initial access period to minimize 10-year retention costs.

questions.question:
Shared infrastructure across millions of AWS customers enables dramatically lower per-unit costs than any single company could achieve independently.

Which principle of AWS cloud computing best explains how this cost reduction is achieved?

choices.text: Economies of scale reduce costs by distributing infrastructure expenses across a large number of customers
choices.explanation: This describes the core principle of economies of scale, where AWS infrastructure is shared across millions of customers, allowing the cost per user to be significantly lower than if a single company built its own data centers.

choices.text: AWS automatically compresses data in transit to reduce bandwidth costs
choices.explanation: Data compression is a technical optimization, but it is not the principle of economies of scale. Economies of scale refers to cost advantages from scale and shared resource utilization, not compression techniques.

choices.text: On-demand capacity provisioning allows customers to scale resources without capital expenditure
choices.explanation: On-demand provisioning provides flexibility but does not explain the underlying economies of scale. The cost reduction from economies of scale comes from AWS spreading infrastructure costs across millions of users, not just from avoiding capital expenditure.

choices.text: Pay-as-you-go pricing eliminates all upfront infrastructure investment
choices.explanation: While pay-as-you-go is an advantage, it does not specifically address the economies of scale principle. This is about billing flexibility, not about cost reduction through shared resources across many customers.

skills: 1.1.1: Understanding the economies of scale (for example, cost savings).
questions.tip: Think about how AWS achieves lower per-unit costs compared to a single company building its own infrastructure. What advantage comes from AWS serving millions of customers?
questions.explanation:
AWS achieves economies of scale by building and maintaining shared infrastructure that serves millions of customers worldwide.

**Why it works:** By distributing capital and operational costs across a massive customer base, AWS can achieve dramatically lower per-unit costs than any individual company could achieve independently. This allows customers to benefit from AWS's scale without bearing the full cost burden.

**Why the others fail:**
- Pay-as-you-go pricing describes a billing model, not the underlying cost advantage from scale and shared resources.
- Automatic data compression is a technical feature, not the principle of economies of scale.
- On-demand provisioning provides operational flexibility but does not explain how AWS achieves lower absolute costs through shared infrastructure.

**Implementation:** AWS benefits all customers automatically through shared infrastructure; no specific configuration is required.

questions.question:
Two database options are under evaluation: purchasing and maintaining on-premises servers versus using Amazon RDS with reserved instances.

How does the economies of scale principle impact the total cost of ownership in this decision?

choices.text: AWS spreads infrastructure, power, and operational costs across millions of customers, reducing the per-instance cost
choices.explanation: This directly applies the economies of scale principle. AWS leverages the shared infrastructure model, where massive scale enables unit economics far better than on-premises solutions. The company benefits from AWS's ability to amortize costs across a global customer base.

choices.text: On-premises servers cost more because they require larger amounts of RAM and storage capacity
choices.explanation: This is incorrect. On-premises servers cost more primarily due to the lack of economies of scale, not because they require larger hardware specifications. The architect would size both solutions appropriately for the workload.

choices.text: Reserved instances guarantee 100% uptime and eliminate the need for backup systems
choices.explanation: Reserved instances provide cost savings through commitment-based pricing, but they do not directly address economies of scale. Additionally, reserved instances do not provide a 100% uptime guarantee or eliminate the need for backups.

choices.text: Cloud databases are always more expensive because AWS charges monthly subscription fees
choices.explanation: This contradicts the premise of economies of scale. Cloud databases are typically cheaper due to shared infrastructure and operational efficiency, and AWS pricing is typically lower than the equivalent on-premises total cost of ownership.

skills: 1.1.1: Understanding the economies of scale (for example, cost savings).
questions.tip: Consider how the cost per customer database instance changes when AWS runs databases for millions of customers versus a company running databases only for itself.
questions.explanation:
The economies of scale principle is fundamental to AWS cost advantages over on-premises infrastructure.

**Why it works:** AWS amortizes its massive infrastructure, real estate, power, cooling, and staffing costs across millions of customers globally. This allows the cost per customer to be significantly lower than any individual organization could achieve managing their own data centers. Amazon RDS exemplifies this by offering managed database instances at a fraction of the cost of equivalent on-premises deployments when total cost of ownership—including management, patching, backups, and redundancy—is calculated.

**Why the others fail:**
- Reserved instances provide pricing discounts through commitment, not through economies of scale.
- On-premises infrastructure costs more due to lack of scale and shared resource distribution, not due to larger hardware requirements.
- Cloud databases are typically cheaper than on-premises due to economies of scale, not more expensive.

**Implementation:** Leverage AWS managed services and reserved instances to maximize the economies of scale benefits. Consult the AWS Pricing Calculator to compare on-premises TCO with RDS costs.

questions.question:
Large volumes of backup data accumulate over time and must be kept for legal compliance, but the data is rarely accessed after the first few months. Manual deletion and archival are time-consuming and error-prone.

How can lifecycle policies improve this scenario?

choices.text: Prevent accidental deletion of objects in the bucket
choices.explanation: Object protection is provided by MFA Delete or bucket versioning, not lifecycle policies.

choices.text: Automatically delete or archive data based on configurable age rules without manual intervention
choices.explanation: Lifecycle policies eliminate manual archive and deletion tasks by automatically transitioning or removing objects based on time-based rules.

choices.text: Enable real-time access to archived files instantly
choices.explanation: Archived data in Glacier requires retrieval time (minutes to hours); lifecycle policies do not provide instant access.

choices.text: Increase the number of replicas stored across regions
choices.explanation: Data replication is controlled by cross-region replication settings, not lifecycle policies.

skills: 3.6.6: Understanding use cases for lifecycle policies.
questions.tip: Think about automating data management tasks to improve compliance and reduce operational overhead.
questions.explanation:
Lifecycle policies automate data management by applying rules consistently without manual effort.

**Why it works:** Rules can automatically transition old backups to cheaper tiers (Glacier) or delete them entirely when they reach a specified age, ensuring compliance and cost optimization.

**Why the others fail:**
- Replication: Configured separately via cross-region replication settings
- Instant retrieval: Glacier requires restoration time; lifecycle policies cannot bypass this
- Deletion protection: Managed through versioning and MFA Delete, separate from lifecycle rules

**Implementation:** Define lifecycle rules to archive backups after 90 days and delete after 7 years to balance compliance and cost.

questions.question:
Storage costs must be optimized across data sets with unpredictable access patterns — some objects are frequently accessed, while others vary in usage over time.

Which TWO pricing strategies help reduce total storage costs?

choices.text: Implement lifecycle policies to transition objects to cheaper tiers as they age
choices.explanation: Lifecycle transitions reduce storage costs by moving infrequently accessed data from Standard to Standard-IA, Glacier, or Deep Archive.

choices.text: Use AWS Backup for all S3 object storage
choices.explanation: AWS Backup is for incremental backup snapshots, not a storage cost optimization for S3 objects.

choices.text: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering to automatically move objects between tiers based on access patterns
choices.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering eliminates the need to manually transition objects and saves 70% on storage for variable access patterns.

choices.text: Enable cross-region replication to all objects
choices.explanation: Replication increases costs; it improves availability, not storage cost optimization.

choices.text: Store all data in S3 Standard and manually delete old files
choices.explanation: Manual deletion is error-prone and Standard doesn't optimize costs; lifecycle automation is better.

skills: 4.1.5: Understanding different pricing options for various storage options and tiers.
questions.tip: Combine automatic tier management and age-based transitions for maximum cost savings across mixed access patterns.
questions.explanation:
Intelligent-Tiering and lifecycle policies together optimize costs by automating storage class selection.

**Why they work:** Intelligent-Tiering handles unpredictable access automatically; lifecycle policies provide predictable rules for aging data.

**Why the others fail:**
- Manual deletion: Error-prone and doesn't utilize cheaper storage classes
- AWS Backup: Designed for incremental snapshots, not S3 object storage optimization
- Cross-region replication: Doubles costs and is for disaster recovery, not optimization

**Implementation:** Combine Intelligent-Tiering for active objects with lifecycle policies to transition older objects to cheaper classes.

questions.question:
Comparing cloud costs with on-premises infrastructure expenses reveals hidden costs that exist on-premises but disappear in AWS.

Which hidden cost is typically NOT incurred in AWS but IS a significant expense in an on-premises data center?

choices.text: Per-request API call charges
choices.explanation: API calls are charged in AWS, not a unique benefit over on-premises.

choices.text: Data transfer between availability zones
choices.explanation: Zone transfer is an AWS cost that on-premises avoids, but it's typically minimal compared to infrastructure costs.

choices.text: Hardware replacement and refresh cycles
choices.explanation: On-premises requires periodic hardware replacement due to obsolescence and technology cycles, but AWS provides automatically maintained infrastructure.

choices.text: Monthly storage service fees
choices.explanation: Storage fees are charged in both AWS and on-premises (for maintenance and space).

skills: 1.4.2: Understanding costs that are associated with on-premises environments.
questions.tip: Think about the long-term capital expenses of maintaining physical equipment versus cloud's operational model.
questions.explanation:
On-premises hardware requires regular replacement cycles, whereas AWS manages infrastructure updates transparently.

**Why it works:** Organizations must budget for periodic server replacement (typically every 3-5 years) and upgrades to stay current with technology.

**Why the others fail:**
- Per-request API charges: AWS has these, on-premises does not; not a cost on-premises avoids
- Storage fees: Both environments incur storage-related costs
- Data transfer: On-premises avoids this, but it's typically a smaller cost component

**Implementation:** Factor hardware refresh cycles into on-premises TCO calculations when comparing to AWS consumption-based pricing.

questions.question:
Evaluating the total cost of ownership (TCO) for migrating from an on-premises data center to AWS requires identifying the major capital expenditures unique to on-premises infrastructure.

Which of the following represents the largest ongoing cost in an on-premises environment?

choices.text: Reserved Instance commitments
choices.explanation: Reserved Instances are an AWS pricing option, not relevant to on-premises costs.

choices.text: AWS data transfer fees
choices.explanation: Data transfer is an AWS cloud cost, not an on-premises cost.

choices.text: Physical infrastructure maintenance and facility costs
choices.explanation: On-premises environments require continuous spending on physical servers, cooling, power, and facility management.

choices.text: Subscription licensing for cloud services
choices.explanation: Cloud subscriptions are not applicable to on-premises environments.

skills: 1.4.2: Understanding costs that are associated with on-premises environments.
questions.tip: Consider the physical and operational expenses unique to managing hardware and facilities in a data center.
questions.explanation:
On-premises infrastructure requires substantial ongoing costs for physical infrastructure maintenance, facility operations, and management.

**Why it works:** Organizations must pay for server hardware deprecation, cooling systems, power consumption, physical space, and IT staff to manage the data center.

**Why the others fail:**
- AWS data transfer fees: These are cloud-specific costs, not on-premises costs
- Reserved Instance commitments: AWS pricing model, not applicable to on-premises
- Cloud service subscriptions: Only relevant to cloud-based operations, not on-premises

**Implementation:** Compare on-premises capital and operational expenses with AWS monthly consumption costs to determine TCO benefits.

questions.question:
Three distinct access tiers define the data lifecycle: frequently accessed databases (first 3 months), occasionally accessed archives (3–12 months), and rarely accessed long-term compliance records (beyond 1 year). Both cost and performance must be optimized.

Which TWO lifecycle policy strategies address this?

choices.text: Keep all data in S3 Standard to ensure instant access regardless of cost
choices.explanation: This defeats the purpose of lifecycle policies and does not optimize for cost savings.

choices.text: Transition recent objects to S3 Intelligent-Tiering for automatic tier management based on access
choices.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between tiers based on changing access patterns without manual rules.

choices.text: Use versioning to maintain multiple copies of each object
choices.explanation: Versioning is a data protection feature, not a lifecycle management strategy for cost optimization.

choices.text: Implement cross-region replication to reduce access latency
choices.explanation: Replication improves availability but is not a lifecycle transition strategy.

choices.text: Move objects older than 1 year to S3 Glacier Deep Archive for cost-effective long-term compliance storage
choices.explanation: Deep Archive provides 99.999999999% durability at minimal cost for data that rarely requires access.

skills: 3.6.6: Understanding use cases for lifecycle policies.
questions.tip: Consider combining automatic tier management with archival strategies to balance access performance and storage costs.
questions.explanation:
Multi-tier lifecycle policies optimize cost and performance by matching storage class to access frequency.

**Why they work:** S3 Intelligent-Tiering handles frequent/occasional access automatically; Deep Archive provides low-cost long-term storage when access is minimal.

**Why the others fail:**
- S3 Standard everywhere: Wastes money on expensive storage for rarely accessed data
- Cross-region replication: Increases cost and doesn't automate tier transitions
- Versioning: Provides protection but increases storage costs without cost optimization

**Implementation:** Create lifecycle rules: transition to Intelligent-Tiering at 3 months, then move to Deep Archive at 12 months for multi-tier cost optimization.

questions.question:
Log files in Amazon S3 are frequently accessed during the first month but rarely accessed afterward. Storage costs must be reduced while maintaining compliance with a 7-year retention requirement.

Which use case best describes the application of S3 lifecycle policies?

choices.text: Compressing objects to reduce bandwidth usage
choices.explanation: Object compression must be done before upload; lifecycle policies do not perform compression.

choices.text: Automatically transitioning objects to cheaper storage classes and archiving old data
choices.explanation: Lifecycle policies can automatically move objects to Glacier or Deep Archive for long-term retention at lower costs.

choices.text: Encrypting all objects in the bucket at rest
choices.explanation: Encryption is a separate S3 feature and not the purpose of lifecycle policies.

choices.text: Restricting public access to objects based on age
choices.explanation: Access control is managed by bucket policies and IAM, not lifecycle policies.

skills: 3.6.6: Understanding use cases for lifecycle policies.
questions.tip: Consider how to optimize storage costs while meeting regulatory data retention requirements.
questions.explanation:
S3 lifecycle policies automatically transition objects between storage classes to optimize costs based on access patterns.

**Why it works:** Policies can move objects from S3 Standard (hot) → S3 Intelligent-Tiering → Glacier (warm) → Deep Archive (cold) as they age, reducing storage costs significantly.

**Why the others fail:**
- Encryption: Managed separately via server-side encryption settings, not lifecycle policies
- Access restrictions: Controlled by bucket policies and IAM, not object age rules
- Compression: Pre-processing task, not automated by lifecycle policies

**Implementation:** Create an S3 lifecycle policy in the bucket settings to transition objects after 30 days to Glacier and after 1 year to Deep Archive.

questions.question:
Protecting a web application from SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks requires a solution that operates at the application layer.

Which security service should be implemented?

choices.text: AWS Shield Standard
choices.explanation: AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks, not application vulnerabilities like SQL injection or XSS.

choices.text: AWS WAF
choices.explanation: AWS WAF protects web applications from common web exploits by filtering malicious requests at the application layer.

choices.text: Network ACLs
choices.explanation: Network ACLs filter traffic at the network layer and cannot inspect application-layer attack patterns.

choices.text: Security Groups
choices.explanation: Security Groups control network-level access but cannot detect or prevent application-layer attacks like SQL injection.

skills: 2.2.3: Describing how customers secure resources on AWS (for example, Amazon Inspector, AWS Security Hub, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Shield).
questions.tip: Think about which layer of the OSI model addresses application-specific threats like SQL injection.
questions.explanation:
AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) is designed to protect web applications from application-layer attacks.

**Why it works:** WAF uses rules to inspect HTTP/HTTPS requests and block traffic matching malicious patterns before it reaches the application.

**Why the others fail:**
- Security Groups: Operate at network layer (Layer 4), cannot inspect application content
- Network ACLs: Also operate at network layer, cannot detect web-specific attack patterns
- AWS Shield: Defends against volumetric DDoS attacks, not targeted application exploits

**Implementation:** Deploy AWS WAF in front of CloudFront distributions, ALBs, or API Gateway to filter web traffic.

questions.question:
Frequently accessed data requiring low-latency retrieval must be stored in S3. The data is accessed regularly throughout the week, and cost optimization is a concern.

Which S3 storage class offers the best balance between access speed and cost for this scenario?

choices.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive
choices.explanation: Deep Archive is the cheapest option but has 12-hour retrieval time; unsuitable for frequent access.

choices.text: S3 Standard
choices.explanation: S3 Standard provides instant retrieval with the lowest access latency, ideal for frequently accessed data.

choices.text: S3 Standard-IA
choices.explanation: Standard-IA has retrieval time delays and is designed for infrequent access with lower storage costs.

choices.text: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
choices.explanation: Glacier Instant is cheaper but targets infrequent access (quarterly); not ideal for frequent weekly access.

skills: 4.1.5: Understanding different pricing options for various storage options and tiers.
questions.tip: Match the storage class to the access frequency: standard for frequent, infrequent-access tiers for older data.
questions.explanation:
S3 Standard provides the fastest access with minimal latency, making it optimal for active workloads.

**Why it works:** Standard-class objects are immediately available, providing millisecond latency for frequently accessed data.

**Why the others fail:**
- Glacier Instant: Lower cost but designed for quarterly access patterns, not weekly access
- Standard-IA: Designed for infrequent access; retrieval takes time and incurs retrieval fees
- Deep Archive: Lowest cost but 12-hour retrieval time makes it unsuitable for frequent access

**Implementation:** Store frequently accessed data in S3 Standard; consider lifecycle transitions to Standard-IA after 30 days of inactivity.

questions.question:
Mission-critical applications on AWS directly impact revenue. Required: a 15-minute response time for critical issues and a dedicated technical account manager (TAM) for AWS architecture guidance.

Which support plan provides the best fit?

choices.text: AWS Enterprise On-Ramp Support
choices.explanation: Enterprise On-Ramp provides 30-minute response for urgent issues and includes access to a TAM for architecture guidance.

choices.text: AWS Basic Support
choices.explanation: Basic Support does not include TAM or priority response times.

choices.text: AWS Developer Support
choices.explanation: Developer Support does not include dedicated TAM or critical response time guarantees.

choices.text: AWS Business Support
choices.explanation: Business Support has 1-hour response time for critical issues, slower than the 15-minute requirement.

skills: 3.8.4: Choosing the appropriate option for business support assistance.
questions.tip: Consider the balance between response time SLA and dedicated support resources like a TAM.
questions.explanation:
AWS Enterprise On-Ramp Support balances cost and coverage, providing 30-minute response with TAM support.

**Why it works:** Enterprise On-Ramp includes a dedicated TAM for proactive guidance and 30-minute response for urgent issues.

**Why the others fail:**
- Business Support: 1-hour response is slower; no dedicated TAM
- Basic Support: No technical support or architecture guidance
- Developer Support: No TAM or critical response guarantees

**Implementation:** Evaluate both Enterprise On-Ramp (30-min SLA) and Enterprise (15-min SLA) based on your critical issue response needs.

questions.question:
Designing a security strategy across multiple AWS services requires identifying which responsibilities belong to the customer versus AWS.

Which TWO of the following are customer responsibilities in the AWS Shared Responsibility Model?

choices.text: Applying security updates to guest operating systems and applications running on EC2
choices.explanation: Customers are responsible for patching the guest OS and all applications they deploy on their instances.

choices.text: Encrypting data in transit between client applications and AWS services
choices.explanation: While AWS provides encryption tools like TLS/SSL, customers must enable and configure encryption for their specific data flows; this is primarily AWS responsibility for the transport layer between services.

choices.text: Maintaining physical network infrastructure and connecting AWS data centers
choices.explanation: AWS maintains all physical network infrastructure, undersea cables, and inter-data center connections.

choices.text: Configuring AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and user access controls
choices.explanation: Customers must design and implement IAM policies, user roles, and access control strategies appropriate for their organization.

choices.text: Managing security patches for the host operating system and virtualization layer
choices.explanation: AWS manages the hypervisor, host OS patches, and virtualization infrastructure; this is AWS responsibility, not customer responsibility.

skills: 2.1.1: Recognizing the components of the AWS shared responsibility model.
questions.tip: Focus on decisions and configurations customers make versus infrastructure AWS maintains.
questions.explanation:
The shared responsibility model divides security concerns: AWS manages the infrastructure layer (physical facilities, hypervisors, networking), while customers manage access controls and their deployed resources.

**Why the correct answers work:**
- IAM configuration: Customers design and implement access control policies tailored to their organization.
- Guest OS patching: Customers own responsibility for patching their deployed operating systems and applications.

**Why the others fail:**
- Host OS/hypervisor patches: AWS manages all host-level infrastructure and hypervisor updates.
- Physical network infrastructure: AWS maintains data centers, cables, and inter-datacenter connections.
- Client-to-AWS encryption: While customers enable encryption, the underlying transport infrastructure is AWS responsibility.

**Implementation:** Set up IAM users and policies via AWS Console > IAM > Users/Roles or use `aws iam create-user` and `aws iam put-user-policy`. Update EC2 instances with `sudo yum update` or `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade` for guest OS patches.

questions.question:
Technical support with a maximum 1-hour response time for production issues is required for a production web application on AWS. The team prefers cost-effective coverage.

Which AWS Support plan best meets these requirements?

choices.text: AWS Basic Support

AWS Business Support provides 1-hour response time for production issues, meeting the startup's requirements at a reasonable cost.

**Why it works:** Business Support guarantees 1-hour response for production issues and includes API access, unlimited service tickets, and 24/7 support.

**Why the others fail:**
- Developer Support: Provides 12-24 hour response time, slower than required
- Enterprise Support: Overkill for startup needs with much higher costs
- Basic Support: No technical support for production issues

questions.question:
Cost advantages emerge across several areas when migrating from on-premises to AWS.

Which TWO cost areas demonstrate significant savings?

choices.text: Reduction of operational expenses for facility management and infrastructure maintenance
choices.explanation: AWS removes costs for power, cooling, space, security, and IT staff dedicated to hardware management.

choices.text: Elimination of software licensing fees
choices.explanation: AWS does not eliminate software licensing; some costs shift but licensing is still required for applications.

choices.text: Guaranteed reduction in network bandwidth costs
choices.explanation: Network costs may vary in AWS depending on data transfer patterns; not guaranteed to be lower.

choices.text: Lower costs from increased redundancy and backup solutions
choices.explanation: While AWS provides better availability, this is a benefit rather than a cost savings from reduced redundancy.

choices.text: Elimination of capital expenditure for physical hardware purchases
choices.explanation: AWS eliminates upfront costs for servers, storage arrays, and networking equipment that on-premises requires.

skills: 1.4.2: Understanding costs that are associated with on-premises environments.
questions.tip: Focus on the structural cost differences between maintaining physical infrastructure and using cloud services.
questions.explanation:
The primary cost advantages of cloud migration come from eliminating capital hardware costs and reducing operational infrastructure expenses.

**Why they work:** On-premises requires upfront capital for hardware and ongoing facility/staffing costs that AWS converts to consumption-based operational expenses.

**Why the others fail:**
- Redundancy costs: AWS provides better availability but this is a feature benefit, not a cost reduction
- Software licensing: Licensing requirements don't change with cloud migration
- Bandwidth costs: These vary case-by-case and are not guaranteed to decrease

**Implementation:** Build TCO models comparing on-premises capital and operational expenses against AWS monthly consumption costs to quantify savings.

questions.question:
A security engineer has deployed a Lambda rotation function using the `SecretsManagerRDSMySQLRotationSingleUser` template for a secret named `prod/db/master-credentials`. The engineer runs the following command to associate the rotation function with the secret:

`aws secretsmanager rotate-secret --secret-id prod/db/master-credentials --rotation-lambda-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:MyRotationFn`

The command completes successfully and an immediate rotation occurs, but the secret is never rotated automatically again.

Which command should the engineer run to configure a 30-day automatic rotation schedule without triggering another immediate rotation?

choices.text:
aws secretsmanager rotate-secret \
  --secret-id prod/db/master-credentials \
  --rotation-lambda-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:MyRotationFn \
  --rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=30 \
  --no-rotate-immediately
choices.explanation: The `rotate-secret` subcommand manages both the rotation Lambda association and the rotation schedule. The `--rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=30` parameter sets up the 30-day recurring schedule. By default, `rotate-secret` also invokes the Lambda immediately - adding `--no-rotate-immediately` suppresses that invocation so the schedule is updated without consuming another rotation cycle.

choices.text:
aws secretsmanager update-secret \
  --secret-id prod/db/master-credentials \
  --rotation-lambda-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:MyRotationFn \
  --rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=30 \
  --rotation-enabled true
choices.explanation: The `update-secret` subcommand modifies secret metadata such as description, KMS key, or secret value. It does not accept `--rotation-lambda-arn`, `--rotation-rules`, or `--rotation-enabled` parameters. Rotation configuration including the Lambda ARN and schedule is managed exclusively through the `rotate-secret` subcommand.

choices.text:
aws secretsmanager create-rotation-schedule \
  --secret-id prod/db/master-credentials \
  --lambda-function-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:MyRotationFn \
  --schedule-expression 'rate(30 days)' \
  --rotation-enabled true
choices.explanation: There is no `create-rotation-schedule` subcommand in the AWS Secrets Manager CLI, and Secrets Manager rotation does not accept EventBridge-style rate expressions. Rotation frequency is specified as an integer number of days via the `--rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=N` parameter of the `rotate-secret` subcommand.

choices.text:
aws secretsmanager put-rotation-configuration \
  --secret-id prod/db/master-credentials \
  --rotation-function-arn arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:123456789012:function:MyRotationFn \
  --automatically-after-days 30 \
  --enable-rotation
choices.explanation: There is no `put-rotation-configuration` subcommand in the AWS Secrets Manager CLI. This command would fail with an unknown command error. Rotation scheduling is configured exclusively using the `rotate-secret` subcommand with the `--rotation-rules` parameter.

skills: 5.3.1: Design management and rotation of credentials and secrets (for example, AWS Secrets Manager).
questions.tip: Both the rotation Lambda association and the rotation schedule are controlled by a single Secrets Manager CLI subcommand. Look for a parameter that sets the recurrence interval and a flag that decouples the configuration update from triggering an immediate rotation cycle.
questions.explanation:
The `rotate-secret` subcommand is the correct tool for both associating a rotation Lambda and configuring a recurrence schedule.

**Why it works:** Without `--rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=N`, Secrets Manager performs a one-time rotation only. Adding `--rotation-rules AutomaticallyAfterDays=30` sets the recurring 30-day schedule. The `--no-rotate-immediately` flag suppresses the default immediate Lambda invocation, updating only the schedule without consuming a rotation cycle.

**Why the others fail:**
- `update-secret`: does not accept rotation parameters - rotation configuration is managed exclusively through `rotate-secret`.
- `put-rotation-configuration`: does not exist in the Secrets Manager CLI.
- `create-rotation-schedule`: does not exist; Secrets Manager does not accept EventBridge-style rate expressions.

**Implementation:** After running the command, verify with `aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id prod/db/master-credentials` and inspect the `RotationEnabled`, `RotationRules`, and `NextRotationDate` fields.

questions.question: The detection layer of a large enterprise AWS environment relies on different native services for different threat types. Match each detection requirement to the AWS security service that best satisfies it.

choices.text: AWS Security Hub
choices.explanation: Security Hub aggregates findings from integrated services (GuardDuty, Macie, Inspector, Config, etc.), maps them to compliance framework controls (CIS, PCI DSS, NIST 800-53), and computes a consolidated security score per account and region - exactly the correlation and scoring use case described.

choices.text: Amazon Security Lake
choices.explanation: Security Lake automatically collects, transforms, and normalizes security data from AWS services and third-party sources into the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) format, storing it in S3 in Parquet for scalable, long-term analysis. It is purpose-built for the data lake use case.

choices.text: Amazon GuardDuty
choices.explanation: GuardDuty continuously analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs using threat intelligence feeds. It has built-in detection for Tor-related activity (finding type: `UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/TorIPCaller`) and other network-based anomalies without any configuration beyond enablement.

choices.text: Amazon Macie
choices.explanation: Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover sensitive data - including PCI DSS payment card numbers - within S3 objects. It produces per-bucket and per-object findings with the specific sensitive data type detected, making it the right tool for data classification requirements.

slots.label: Aggregate and normalize findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and Macie into a single OCSF-formatted data lake for long-term analysis
Identify S3 buckets that contain unencrypted payment card numbers
Detect IAM credentials being used from a Tor exit node
Correlate findings across multiple AWS security services and apply compliance framework controls to produce a consolidated security score

skills: 1.1.4: Create metrics, alerts, and dashboards to detect anomalous data and events (for example, Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Security Lake, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Macie).
questions.tip: Consider each service's primary design purpose: threat detection, data classification, finding aggregation/scoring, or security data lake.
questions.explanation:
Each service has a distinct primary function in the detection layer.

**Why it works:**
- GuardDuty: threat intelligence and behavioral detection - identifies malicious network activity including Tor-based credential use (`UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/TorIPCaller`) from integrated log sources.
- Macie: sensitive data discovery for S3, detecting PCI, PII, and other regulated data categories using ML and pattern matching.
- Security Hub: aggregation and compliance posture layer - imports findings, maps them to control frameworks, and scores security posture.
- Security Lake: OCSF-normalized security data lake - centralized, long-term retention and analysis across AWS and third-party sources.

questions.question:
A security operations team has enabled Amazon GuardDuty across all accounts in an AWS Organization. The team wants to receive a Slack notification within five minutes whenever GuardDuty generates a HIGH severity finding in any member account. The solution must require no additional infrastructure to poll for findings.

Which approach delivers near-real-time Slack alerts with the least operational overhead?

choices.text: Create a CloudWatch Metrics Alarm on the GuardDuty finding count metric filtered by HIGH severity, set an SNS action, and subscribe Lambda to the SNS topic.
choices.explanation: GuardDuty doesn't publish a standard CloudWatch metric for finding severity, so there's nothing to alarm on. CloudWatch Metric Alarms also have a minimum evaluation period of 60 seconds with no finer granularity. EventBridge is the purpose-built real-time routing mechanism for GuardDuty findings.

choices.text: Enable AWS Security Hub in the administrator account, configure Security Hub to forward HIGH findings to an SNS topic, and subscribe the Slack webhook URL directly to the SNS topic.
choices.explanation: SNS doesn't natively support Slack webhooks as a subscription protocol, so you'd still need Lambda in the middle. On top of that, routing through Security Hub adds an unnecessary hop (GuardDuty → Security Hub → SNS → Lambda) when EventBridge handles the whole thing directly.

choices.text: Enable GuardDuty S3 export, configure an S3 event notification to trigger Lambda when new finding files arrive, and post to Slack from Lambda.
choices.explanation: GuardDuty S3 export uses GZIP-compressed NDJSON files that get delivered periodically (every 6 hours by default for active findings). That's way too slow for a 5-minute alerting requirement and completely misses the real-time EventBridge stream.

choices.text: Create an EventBridge rule in the GuardDuty delegated administrator account that matches GuardDuty findings with severity >= 7, invoke a Lambda function as the target, and have the function post to a Slack webhook.
choices.explanation: GuardDuty publishes findings as EventBridge events in near-real time. A single EventBridge rule in the delegated administrator account picks up aggregated findings from all member accounts. Filtering on `severity >= 7` limits it to HIGH findings only. Lambda handles the Slack webhook call with no polling infrastructure needed.

skills: 1.1.4: Create metrics, alerts, and dashboards to detect anomalous data and events (for example, Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Security Lake, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Macie).
questions.tip: You want instant notifications, not batch reports delivered hours later. Which service gives you real-time event delivery from GuardDuty?
questions.explanation:
GuardDuty has a direct pipeline to EventBridge. When it detects something suspicious it fires an event within minutes. Since you want alerts from all member accounts, set up the rule in your delegated administrator account where findings from everywhere get aggregated.

**The setup is straightforward:** create an EventBridge rule that filters for `severity >= 7` (this catches HIGH findings at 7–8.9 and CRITICAL at 9+), then wire it to a Lambda function that posts to your Slack webhook. Sub-minute latency with zero infrastructure to manage.

**Why the other options miss the mark:**
- S3 export is batch-oriented and can take up to 6 hours to deliver
- Security Hub adds an unnecessary extra hop and you'd still need Lambda anyway
- CloudWatch doesn't have per-finding severity metrics for GuardDuty

The EventBridge approach is both the simplest and the fastest option here.

questions.question:
A financial services company enables Amazon Macie to monitor all S3 buckets for sensitive data exposure. After a week, the security team notices that Macie is generating hundreds of daily findings for intentionally public marketing asset buckets, obscuring genuine alerts. The team needs to suppress Macie findings for these known-safe buckets while continuing to alert on all other S3 findings.

Which Macie feature directly addresses this without disabling monitoring on those buckets?

choices.text: Create Macie suppression rules that filter findings based on the S3 bucket name, setting the finding status to Suppressed for findings matching the marketing buckets.
choices.explanation: Suppression rules let you filter findings based on criteria like bucket name, finding type, or classification job ARN. Matching findings get automatically archived with a `Suppressed` status. They still exist in Macie for audit purposes but they're hidden from the active findings view and won't trigger downstream EventBridge events.

choices.text: Add the marketing buckets to the Macie allow list so that sensitive data detected in those buckets is not reported as a finding.
choices.explanation: Allow lists suppress findings for specific text patterns or regular expressions, like known test credit card numbers. They don't suppress all findings for an entire bucket. If those marketing buckets contained real sensitive data outside the allow list pattern, Macie would still flag it.

choices.text: Publish all Macie findings to Security Hub and create a Security Hub suppression filter scoped to the marketing bucket ARNs.
choices.explanation: Security Hub suppression filters work on findings after they arrive in Security Hub and do hide them from the Security Hub console. But the findings still show up in the native Macie console and still trigger EventBridge events. Suppressing at the Macie layer with suppression rules is more thorough.

choices.text: Disable the Macie classification job for the marketing buckets and enable it only for remaining buckets.
choices.explanation: Disabling a classification job stops Macie from scanning those buckets entirely so you'd lose all visibility. Suppression rules are the better approach because they keep the audit trail and still run discovery. They just filter the noise out of your operational dashboards.

skills: 1.1.4: Create metrics, alerts, and dashboards to detect anomalous data and events (for example, Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Security Lake, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Macie).
questions.tip: You need to quiet the noise from buckets you know are safe without losing protection everywhere else. What Macie feature lets you selectively hide findings?
questions.explanation:
Suppression rules are purpose-built for exactly this scenario. You tell Macie "stop showing me findings from these specific buckets" and it marks them as `Suppressed`. They're still logged for audit purposes, but they vanish from your operational dashboard and won't fire downstream alerts.

**Why the other approaches fall short:**
- Allow lists work on text patterns, not whole buckets. If those marketing buckets accidentally contained real sensitive data outside the allowed pattern, you'd still get findings.
- Disabling classification jobs kills monitoring entirely and you lose all visibility, which isn't the goal.
- Security Hub filters only suppress findings within Security Hub itself. The noise persists in Macie and still triggers EventBridge events.

The beauty of suppression rules is they work at the source. Macie applies them before sending findings anywhere else.

questions.question:
Audit logs must be protected from deletion or modification for seven years using S3 Glacier Vault Lock. The enforcement process follows a specific sequence that, once completed, cannot be reversed.

Arrange the following steps in the correct order to complete the Vault Lock policy enforcement process.

choices.text: Call complete-vault-lock with the lock ID to permanently enforce the Compliance-mode policy
choices.explanation: `complete-vault-lock` commits the policy and there's no going back. Once you call it, the policy cannot be changed or deleted by anyone for the entire retention period.

choices.text: Call initiate-vault-lock to attach a policy and receive a lock ID in the In-Progress state
choices.explanation: `initiate-vault-lock` always goes first. It creates the policy in a 24-hour trial window and hands you a lock ID. You can't complete the lock without it.

choices.text: Abort the lock (if policy is incorrect) and restart from initiate-vault-lock with a corrected policy
choices.explanation: `abort-vault-lock` is your escape hatch when validation in step 2 reveals a problem. It cancels the InProgress lock so you can start fresh. If validation passes, you skip this and go straight to `complete-vault-lock`. It's listed last because in the normal flow it's a conditional rollback and the happy path ends at step 3.

choices.text: Validate the policy by testing deny conditions against the vault during the 24-hour window
choices.explanation: The 24-hour InProgress window exists specifically so you can validate your policy. Test your deny conditions before committing. Once a Compliance-mode policy is locked, you can't modify it. Ever.

skills: 5.2.2: Design and configure mechanisms to protect data integrity (for example, S3 Object Lock, S3 Glacier Vault Lock, versioning, digital code signing, file validation)
questions.tip: Vault Lock is like signing a contract: there's a review period where you can still back out and then it becomes permanent. What order makes sense?
questions.explanation:
Vault Lock has deliberate safety steps built in to prevent accidents.

You start by initiating the lock with a draft policy. This gives you a 24-hour window where the vault is in "InProgress" state and you can test everything. During this time, run your deny conditions against the vault to confirm the policy behaves as expected.

If everything checks out, complete the vault lock to make it permanent. After that, nobody, not even root users, can change or delete the policy for the entire retention period. That's real compliance-grade immutability.

But if you spot a problem during testing? Use `abort-vault-lock` to tear it all down and start over. This escape hatch only exists during that initial 24-hour window.

The safe deployment pattern is always: initiate → test thoroughly → complete (or abort if something's off).

questions.question:
A compliance engineer must lock a Glacier vault's access policy to enforce a 10-year retention requirement for archived medical records. The vault and an InProgress vault lock policy have already been created. The engineer must complete the lock using the AWS CLI and only has the lock ID from the `initiate-vault-lock` response.

Which command correctly completes the vault lock?

choices.text:
aws glacier set-vault-access-policy \
  --account-id - \
  --vault-name medical-records-vault \
  --policy file://lock-policy.json
choices.explanation: `set-vault-access-policy` manages the standard (mutable) access policy on a vault and has nothing to do with the vault lock mechanism. It won't transition your InProgress lock to the Locked state, and policies set this way can be changed at any time. Not what you need for compliance.

choices.text:
aws glacier put-vault-lock \
  --account-id - \
  --vault-name medical-records-vault \
  --lock-id <lockId>
choices.explanation: `put-vault-lock` doesn't exist in the Glacier CLI. The correct two-step process goes `initiate-vault-lock` (creates the InProgress policy and gives you a lock ID) then `complete-vault-lock` (finalizes it permanently). Running a nonexistent subcommand just returns an error.

choices.text:
aws glacier complete-vault-lock \
  --account-id - \
  --vault-name medical-records-vault \
  --lock-id <lockId>
choices.explanation: `complete-vault-lock` moves the vault lock from InProgress to the permanent Locked state using the lock ID you got from `initiate-vault-lock`. The `--account-id -` flag tells the CLI to use your current account. Once locked, the policy becomes truly immutable and nobody can delete or modify it.

choices.text:
aws glacier initiate-vault-lock \
  --account-id - \
  --vault-name medical-records-vault \
  --policy file://lock-policy.json
choices.explanation: `initiate-vault-lock` starts a new InProgress vault lock, but you've already done that step. Running it again would abort your existing InProgress policy and restart the 24-hour completion window from scratch, which is the opposite of what you want.

skills: 5.2.2: Design and configure mechanisms to protect data integrity (for example, S3 Object Lock, S3 Glacier Vault Lock, versioning, digital code signing, file validation)
questions.tip: Glacier Vault Lock is a two-phase process: you start it then finalize it. Which phase makes the lock permanent?
questions.explanation:
Glacier Vault Lock works in two phases. First, `initiate-vault-lock` creates an InProgress policy and hands you a lock ID, kicking off a 24-hour window to test everything. Then `complete-vault-lock` uses that lock ID to make the policy permanent.

**Why the other commands don't work:**
- `set-vault-access-policy` manages regular mutable access policies. It has nothing to do with the vault lock mechanism.
- Running `initiate-vault-lock` again would abort your existing InProgress lock and reset the 24-hour timer back to zero.
- `put-vault-lock` simply doesn't exist in the Glacier API.

**To complete the lock:** `aws glacier complete-vault-lock --account-id - --vault-name <vault-name> --lock-id <lockId>` (the `--account-id -` flag is required by the Glacier CLI).

questions.question:
A company's central security account stores RDS database credentials in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypted with a customer managed KMS key (CMK). A workload IAM role in a separate application account must retrieve these credentials. The security team has already added the workload role ARN to the Secrets Manager resource-based policy with `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` permission, but every `GetSecretValue` call from the workload account still returns `AccessDeniedException`.

Which configuration must the security engineer apply to resolve the access failure?

choices.text: Update the CMK key policy in the central security account to grant the application account root IAM principal `kms:Decrypt`, enabling IAM identity policies in the application account to independently control CMK access without referencing the workload role ARN directly in the key policy
choices.explanation: Granting the application account root in the CMK key policy does enable IAM delegation for `kms:Decrypt` within that account. However, the workload role's IAM identity policy must still explicitly include `kms:Decrypt` - access is not inherited automatically from the account-root key policy grant. Without that IAM permission the role remains unauthorized and `AccessDeniedException` continues.

choices.text: Update the CMK key policy in the central security account to grant `kms:Decrypt` directly to the workload role ARN, and ensure the workload role's IAM identity policy in the application account includes both `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` and `kms:Decrypt`
choices.explanation: When Secrets Manager retrieves a CMK-encrypted secret for a cross-account caller, it performs `kms:Decrypt` using the calling principal's identity. KMS evaluates the key policy and the caller's IAM policy independently - both must permit the operation. The Secrets Manager resource policy was already configured, so authorization is failing at the KMS layer. Adding the workload role ARN directly to the CMK key policy with `kms:Decrypt`, combined with matching IAM permissions on the workload role, satisfies both checks and resolves the error.

choices.text: Update the CMK key policy in the central security account to add a `kms:ViaService` condition restricting decryption only to the secretsmanager.amazonaws.com service principal, and add a separate key policy statement granting `kms:CreateGrant` to the workload role ARN so it can delegate decrypt permissions
choices.explanation: A `kms:ViaService` condition restricts which service may use the key but does not grant the cross-account principal any authorization. `kms:CreateGrant` allows the holder to delegate specific key operations but does not itself confer `kms:Decrypt` capability. Neither change authorizes the workload role to perform `kms:Decrypt`, so `AccessDeniedException` persists.

choices.text: Update the CMK key policy in the central security account to grant `kms:Decrypt` to the secretsmanager.amazonaws.com service principal for all accounts in the organization using an `aws:PrincipalOrgID` condition key, and use an SCP to restrict `kms:Decrypt` usage to the workload role ARN in the application account
choices.explanation: Granting `kms:Decrypt` to the `secretsmanager.amazonaws.com` service principal org-wide allows any Secrets Manager call within the organization to decrypt secrets, which is excessively permissive and does not authenticate the specific calling IAM role. SCPs are guardrails that restrict what IAM can allow within an account - they cannot grant cross-account permissions to resources in another account. For this reason the approach is both insecure and architecturally incorrect.

skills: 5.3.1: Design management and rotation of credentials and secrets (for example, AWS Secrets Manager).
questions.tip: When cross-account access fails despite the resource policy being configured, identify every independent authorization layer that the API call traverses and verify that each one explicitly grants access to the calling identity.
questions.explanation:
Retrieving a CMK-encrypted secret involves two independent authorization layers: the Secrets Manager resource policy and the KMS key policy.

**Why it works:** AWS KMS does not automatically delegate key authorization to IAM unless the account root or the specific principal is added to the key policy. The Secrets Manager resource policy was already set, so the missing piece is the CMK key policy granting `kms:Decrypt` to the workload role ARN. Additionally, the calling role's own IAM identity policy must explicitly permit both `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` and `kms:Decrypt`.

**Why the others fail:**
- `kms:ViaService` + `kms:CreateGrant`: restricts which service uses the key but does not authorize the cross-account principal to decrypt - `AccessDeniedException` persists.
- Account root grant: enables IAM delegation but still requires an explicit IAM grant on the workload role - incomplete on its own.
- `secretsmanager.amazonaws.com` service principal org-wide: overly permissive; SCPs cannot grant cross-account permissions to resources in another account.

**Implementation:** KMS (central account) > edit CMK key policy > add statement granting `kms:Decrypt` to the workload role ARN. Then update the workload role's IAM policy to include `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` and `kms:Decrypt` scoped to the specific secret ARN and CMK ARN.

questions.question:
A company runs a high-traffic e-commerce application using Amazon RDS PostgreSQL, with database credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager. During a recent credential rotation, application connection errors surged because the Lambda rotation function updated the RDS user password before all active connections using the previous password had closed. The security team needs a rotation strategy that prevents these connection interruptions in future rotations.

Which rotation strategy should the security engineer configure?

choices.text: Configure the single user rotation strategy and enable Amazon RDS Multi-AZ, which automatically promotes a standby database instance before each rotation cycle begins to shield active connection pools from the password update
choices.explanation: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ maintains a synchronous standby replica and promotes it during infrastructure failures. It does not coordinate with Secrets Manager rotation timing. A password change applied to the primary RDS instance is replicated to the standby simultaneously, so enabling Multi-AZ does not create a transition window that preserves old credentials or prevents connection errors during single user rotation.

choices.text: Configure the single user rotation strategy with a drain period by setting a ROTATION_SLEEP_SECONDS Lambda environment variable on the rotation function to delay the password update until existing connections close
choices.explanation: There is no `ROTATION_SLEEP_SECONDS` environment variable in AWS-provided Secrets Manager rotation function templates - this parameter is fabricated. The single user strategy replaces the database user's password atomically, so any connection presenting the old password immediately after rotation fails. Artificial delays reduce but do not eliminate the interruption window and introduce operational fragility.

choices.text: Configure the alternating users rotation strategy, which maintains two dedicated database users and rotates credentials between them, keeping the previous user's credentials valid while existing connections drain
choices.explanation: The alternating users strategy provisions two dedicated database users. While one user's credentials are `AWSCURRENT`, the other user's new credentials are staged as `AWSPENDING`. After promotion, the previously active credentials are retained under the `AWSPREVIOUS` label, allowing in-flight application connections to drain without errors before the old user's password is eventually decommissioned.

choices.text: Configure the single user rotation strategy and set a Lambda reserved concurrency of 1 on the rotation function to serialize invocations, preventing concurrent password updates from disrupting active database sessions across multiple simultaneous callers
choices.explanation: Lambda reserved concurrency limits the number of parallel executions of the rotation function. Secrets Manager invokes the rotation function for a given secret sequentially anyway, so a concurrency limit of 1 has no practical effect. Single user rotation still replaces the password atomically in a single operation, causing connections presenting the old password to fail immediately regardless of invocation concurrency.

skills: 5.3.1: Design management and rotation of credentials and secrets (for example, AWS Secrets Manager).
questions.tip: Consider whether any rotation approach can preserve the previous credentials' validity for a period after the new credentials are activated, eliminating the gap that causes connection errors.
questions.explanation:
The alternating users rotation strategy is designed specifically to eliminate rotation-induced downtime.

**Why it works:** Secrets Manager maintains two database users - one active (`AWSCURRENT`) and one being rotated (`AWSPENDING`). After the new credentials are validated and promoted, the previously active credentials are retained under the `AWSPREVIOUS` label, giving applications with cached connections time to close naturally before the old user is decommissioned.

**Why the others fail:**
- Single user rotation: performs an in-place password replacement with no fallback, creating an immediate gap where old-credential connections fail - artificial delays or concurrency limits do not change this.
- RDS Multi-AZ: a disaster recovery feature entirely independent of Secrets Manager rotation scheduling; password changes replicate to the standby simultaneously.

**Implementation:** Console > Secrets Manager > select the secret > Edit rotation > select "Alternating users" rotation strategy. A superuser secret with permission to modify database user passwords is also required.

questions.question:
An EventBridge rule must match GuardDuty findings of type `UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/SSHBruteForce` with a severity of HIGH or CRITICAL (numeric value 7.0 or above). The rule must match the finding source correctly and avoid triggering on lower-severity variants of the same finding type.

Which EventBridge rule pattern correctly captures these findings?

choices.explanation: GuardDuty severity in EventBridge events is a numeric float (e.g., 7.8), not a string label like `HIGH` or `CRITICAL`. String matching against these labels will never match and the rule will never fire.

The source for GuardDuty EventBridge events is `aws.guardduty`, not `guardduty.amazonaws.com`. Using the wrong source string means the rule will consequently never match any GuardDuty finding regardless of the correct detail filter.

GuardDuty publishes events with source `aws.guardduty` and detail-type `GuardDuty Finding`. The detail block contains the finding type and numeric severity. EventBridge numeric matching with `>=` 7 correctly captures HIGH (7–8.9) and CRITICAL (9+) while excluding MEDIUM and LOW.

The correct detail-type for GuardDuty EventBridge events is `GuardDuty Finding`, not `Security Finding`. `Security Finding` is used by AWS Security Hub for its aggregated findings format (ASFF). Using the wrong detail-type means the rule will not match GuardDuty-native events.

skills: 1.1.4: Create metrics, alerts, and dashboards to detect anomalous data and events (for example, Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Security Lake, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Macie).
questions.tip: Focus on the exact values GuardDuty uses for source, detail-type, and the data type of the severity field in its EventBridge event schema.
questions.explanation:
GuardDuty EventBridge events use: source=`aws.guardduty`, detail-type=`GuardDuty Finding`, and a numeric severity float in the detail object.

**Why it works:** The rule pattern that specifies the correct source, the correct detail-type, and a numeric comparison `>= 7` matches HIGH and CRITICAL findings as intended.

**Why the others fail:**
- One option uses string labels (`HIGH`, `CRITICAL`) for severity which do not match the numeric float field - the rule will consequently never fire.
- Another option uses the wrong source (`guardduty.amazonaws.com` is an API endpoint, not an EventBridge source).
- Another option uses `Security Finding`, which is the Security Hub ASFF detail-type rather than GuardDuty's native `GuardDuty Finding`.

**Implementation:** Console > EventBridge > Rules > Create rule, paste the JSON pattern that uses `aws.guardduty`, `GuardDuty Finding`, and `detail.severity` numeric comparison into the Event pattern editor.

questions.question:
A media company stores master video assets in S3 and requires that accidental overwrites by developers preserve the previous object content and that permanent deletion of any specific version requires multi-factor authentication from the bucket owner. The solution must use native S3 capabilities without restricting the development team's ability to upload new versions.

Which TWO configurations should the security engineer apply?

choices.text: Configure an S3 bucket policy that denies `s3:DeleteObject` for all IAM principals except the bucket owner, and enable S3 Versioning.
choices.explanation: Denying `s3:DeleteObject` via bucket policy blocks deletion of the current object but misses the real target. With versioning enabled, permanent removal requires `s3:DeleteObjectVersion`, which is a completely different action. The policy also doesn't enforce MFA, and the bucket owner can change it whenever they want.

choices.text: Enable MFA Delete on the versioned bucket, requiring the bucket owner to supply a valid MFA code when permanently deleting a specific object version or suspending versioning.
choices.explanation: MFA Delete puts the most destructive S3 operations behind a hardware MFA token that only the bucket owner can provide. Both permanent version deletion and versioning suspension require that MFA code, so no developer or compromised credential can permanently wipe out object history without it.

choices.text: Apply S3 Object Lock in Governance mode with a 90-day retention period and grant all developers the `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` permission for operational flexibility.
choices.explanation: Granting `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` to every developer completely defeats the purpose of Object Lock. On top of that, the fixed retention period would stop developers from correcting accidental uploads, which directly conflicts with their operational needs.

choices.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket so that all PUT operations create a new version rather than overwriting the existing object.
choices.explanation: Versioning turns every overwrite into a new object version instead of replacing what's already there. Developers keep full write access and all original content stays recoverable. Delete operations just add a delete marker and previous versions remain untouched.

choices.text: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication with delete marker replication disabled and rely on the replica bucket as the authoritative copy for recovery.
choices.explanation: CRR copies objects to another region for availability but doesn't stop permanent deletion in the source bucket. Turning off delete marker replication causes the replica to gradually drift out of sync with the source. Neither approach adds MFA enforcement to delete operations.

skills: 5.2.2: Design and configure mechanisms to protect data integrity (for example, S3 Object Lock, S3 Glacier Vault Lock, versioning, digital code signing, file validation)
questions.tip: Think of this as two separate problems: keeping previous versions when files get overwritten, and requiring extra authorization before anything gets permanently deleted.
questions.explanation:
These two features solve different problems. Versioning keeps every object version around so developers can recover anything they accidentally overwrite. MFA Delete locks down the destructive stuff: permanently deleting a version or suspending versioning both require a hardware MFA code from the bucket owner.

**Why the other options fall short:**
- Giving every developer `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` permission completely undermines Object Lock protection.
- A bucket policy denying `s3:DeleteObject` targets the wrong action. With versioning on, you need to block `s3:DeleteObjectVersion` instead and there's no MFA enforcement either.
- Cross-Region Replication provides availability in another region but nothing to prevent deletion at the source.

**To set this up:** `aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket <bucket-name> --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled,MFADelete=Enabled --mfa "<serial-number> <token-code>"` (must be run as the root account).

questions.question:
AWS Security Hub is the central finding aggregation point for a multi-account AWS environment. The team needs a custom insight that surfaces the five S3 buckets with the highest number of CRITICAL severity findings over the past 30 days across all member accounts.

Which TWO actions are required to build this custom insight?

choices.text: Set the workflow status filter to NEW and NOTIFIED to exclude already-remediated findings from the insight results.
choices.explanation: Filtering on `WorkflowStatus` NEW and NOTIFIED keeps the insight focused on open findings rather than resolved ones. That's a nice touch but it's not required to create a working insight. The filter set with grouping attribute plus the aggregation scope are the minimum requirements for what the question describes.

choices.text: Enable Security Hub cross-Region aggregation or ensure the finding aggregator is configured to pull findings from all member account Regions into the administrator account.
choices.explanation: Custom insights can only surface findings that are actually visible in the account and Region where the insight lives. Without cross-account aggregation (delegated administrator with all members enabled) and cross-Region aggregation, findings from member accounts and other Regions simply won't show up in the insight results.

choices.text: Configure each GuardDuty member account to forward findings directly to Security Hub in the administrator account using a GuardDuty cross-account publishing rule.
choices.explanation: GuardDuty findings reach Security Hub through the standard per-account integration, not through some special cross-account publishing rule. The aggregation model goes: GuardDuty → Security Hub (per account) → Security Hub administrator via cross-account membership. There's no direct GuardDuty-to-admin-Security-Hub shortcut.

choices.text: Create an EventBridge rule that matches Security Hub findings, writes them to a DynamoDB table, and query the table to compute the top-five bucket ranking.
choices.explanation: This builds a custom pipeline around Security Hub instead of using the built-in custom insights feature. The question specifically asks about the native capability. Wiring up EventBridge + DynamoDB adds unnecessary complexity and isn't how Security Hub insights work.

choices.text: Define the insight with a filter that sets Severity Label to CRITICAL, Resource Type to AwsS3Bucket, and record state to ACTIVE, then group results by Resource Id.
choices.explanation: Custom insights need a filter set to scope findings (severity, resource type, `RecordState`) and a grouping attribute to aggregate counts. Grouping by `Resource Id` (the bucket ARN) gives you a ranked list of buckets ordered by finding count, which is exactly what the question asks for.

skills: 1.1.4: Create metrics, alerts, and dashboards to detect anomalous data and events (for example, Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Security Lake, AWS Security Hub, Amazon Macie).
questions.tip: Split this into two concerns: what data needs to be visible in your Security Hub account, and how does the insight group that data into a ranked list?
questions.explanation:
You need to solve two problems here.

**First, define the insight itself.** Filter for CRITICAL findings on S3 buckets that are still ACTIVE, then group by Resource ID (the bucket ARN). This gives you a count-based ranking showing which buckets have the most critical issues.

**Second, make sure Security Hub can actually see everything.** Without proper cross-account aggregation (and cross-Region if you're using multiple regions), your insight only shows findings from the local account and region. Pretty useless for a multi-account setup.

**Why the other options miss the mark:**
- Building your own EventBridge + DynamoDB pipeline ignores Security Hub's built-in insights feature
- "GuardDuty cross-account publishing rules" aren't a real thing; findings flow through the standard per-account integration
- Workflow status filtering is a nice-to-have refinement but not required for the basic insight

Once both pieces are in place, Security Hub automatically ranks your buckets by critical finding count.

questions.question: Several distinct data integrity protection requirements exist across an AWS environment. Match each requirement to the AWS feature that best satisfies it.

choices.text: S3 Versioning
choices.explanation: S3 Versioning turns PUT operations into new versions rather than replacements. Any previous version can be restored using its version ID, making accidental overwrites fully recoverable.

choices.text: S3 Object Lock - Compliance mode
choices.explanation: Compliance mode applies WORM protection that nobody can override, not even root, during the retention period. Use this when regulatory mandates like SEC 17a-4 or HIPAA demand absolute immutability.

choices.text: CloudTrail log file validation
choices.explanation: CloudTrail creates hourly SHA-256 digest files and signs them with AWS's private key. When you run `aws cloudtrail validate-logs`, it recomputes the file hashes and checks them against those signed digests. If any log was altered or deleted after delivery, you'll know right away.

choices.text: KMS key deletion cancellation / key policy with DenyScheduleKeyDeletion
choices.explanation: A KMS key policy condition can deny `kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion` and `kms:DisableKey` for all principals during a retention window. This protects the encryption key that your S3 data depends on. If someone deleted the key, all your stored ciphertexts would become permanently unrecoverable.

slots.label: Detect whether a CloudTrail log file was modified or deleted after it was delivered to S3
Ensure a KMS key used for S3 encryption cannot be deleted or disabled during a retention window
Recover a specific earlier version of an S3 object after an accidental overwrite
Prevent S3 objects from being overwritten or deleted for a fixed period, enforced even against the root account

skills: 5.2.2: Design and configure mechanisms to protect data integrity (for example, S3 Object Lock, S3 Glacier Vault Lock, versioning, digital code signing, file validation)
questions.tip: Think about what each control actually protects: is it the data itself, the audit trail, previous versions or the encryption key? Match the control to the right layer.
questions.explanation:
Each control targets a different layer of data integrity.

**Here's how they map:**
- CloudTrail log file validation detects post-delivery tampering of audit logs through signed digests. It proves integrity after the fact without preventing writes.
- S3 Object Lock Compliance mode enforces WORM immutability that no account can override, making it the right tool for hard regulatory retention mandates.
- S3 Versioning preserves every object state so you can do point-in-time recovery after accidental overwrites.
- KMS key policy controls protect the encryption layer. Denying `kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion` and `kms:DisableKey` keeps the key alive. Without it, your encrypted S3 data becomes permanently unreadable.

questions.question:
A security team at a healthcare company suspects that CloudTrail log files stored in their centralized S3 bucket were deleted and recreated with modified content by a compromised administrator account. The team needs a native AWS mechanism that can cryptographically prove whether logs were altered after CloudTrail delivered them to S3.

Which feature provides this capability?

choices.text: AWS Config rule cloudtrail-s3-dataevents-enabled to monitor whether the CloudTrail bucket receives new objects, triggering an SNS alert on anomalies.
choices.explanation: Config managed rules check whether your setup matches compliance standards and can't do cryptographic verification of log file content. This particular rule only checks if data events are enabled, so it tells you nothing about whether delivered logs are genuine or have been tampered with.

choices.text: Amazon Macie configured to scan the CloudTrail S3 bucket for sensitive data patterns and alert when log file sizes deviate from a baseline.
choices.explanation: Macie is built for sensitive data discovery and anomaly detection and doesn't provide cryptographic proof of file integrity. Size-based alerts are heuristic, so if someone modified the content without changing the file size, Macie wouldn't catch it.
